# Bass v. TTUHSC — Litigation Candor Catalog (Public Audit)

This document catalogs specific candor concerns — misstatements of the pleadings, of the record, and of legal authority — identified in filings in *Bass v. Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center* (N.D. Tex. No. 5:25-cv-00244-H-BV; 237th Dist. Ct., Lubbock County, No. DC-2025-CV-1817). Every item has been through an adversarial red-team pass: the strongest available defense of the challenged language is stated, then tested. Only items that survive that test are published here.

**Methodology.** Each item gives (1) the source-text excerpt of what counsel actually wrote, (2) what is wrong with it, (3) the counter-cite or rebuttal anchor, and (4) the red-team test. Items depending on sealed exhibits have those references redacted. Every item quotes the exact filed language and names its source, so any reader can independently check the catalog's characterization against the record.

# Part I

## Federal Docket Candor Catalog


#### F-03 — exhibit_mislabel

- **Severity:** 4 — severe
- **Filing:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27)
- **Signed by:** Scott D. Smith, Assistant Attorney General
- **Location:** p. 3 footnote 2 + accompanying text
- **Rule implicated:** Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(3); Tex. Disciplinary R. 3.03(a)(1)
- **Red-team status:** cleared

**Source-text excerpt (what counsel wrote):**

> Plaintiff was first notified of the consolidated board hearing on November 9, 2023 and a week later he received a second hearing notice informing him the hearing would be held on December 11.

**What is wrong with it:**

Exhibit 1 is captioned 'Notice of Consolidation of Outstanding Student Matters' dated November 9, 2023. The actual Hearing Notice is Exhibit 2, dated November 16, 2023. Different captions, different dates, different functions.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- R2MTD (Doc. 33) at 10
- Tab G C11
- Rule 11 safe-harbor letter item 3

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

- *Strongest defense:* Defense framing: Counsel uses 'Hearing Notice' as colloquial shorthand for both the Nov 9 Notice of Consolidation of Outstanding Student Matters (Ex. 1) and the Nov 16 actual Hearing Notice (Ex. 2). The imprecise label is at most a draftsmanship slip, not a Rule 11(b)(3) factual misstatement, because the rule requires misrepresentation of a material allegation, not loose exhibit captioning.
- *Why it fails:* Doc. 27 fn 2 (L109) deploys the mislabel substantively: 'The November 9, 2023 Hearing Notice informed Plaintiff of a fourth allegation.' WHAT was noticed on Nov 9 is doctrinally load-bearing — it affects the due-process timeline analysis (when was Plaintiff first notified of charges? what was the content of that notice?). Mislabeling the Nov 9 Notice of Consolidation as a 'Hearing Notice' implies notice of charges occurred Nov 9 when in fact the Hearing Notice (Ex. 2, captioned 'Hearing Notice', dated Nov 16) is what provided that information. Material to the timeline argument; not a draftsmanship slip. Three independent rebuttal anchors.
- *Catalog confidence:* 0.85

#### F-02 — phantom_citation

- **Severity:** 4 — severe
- **Filing:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27)

> approved university process.” See TTUHSC OP 77.14, Establishing Reasonable Accommodations for Students with Disabilities, attached as Exhibit 4, at pp. 1-2.

**What is wrong with it:**

Exhibit 4 is TTUHSC OP 77.14 (Establishing Reasonable Accommodations for Students with Disabilities) - a two-page document. Pages 3-17 do not exist. Verifier searched all of Doc. 27's accessible exhibits (Exs. 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12; Exs. 3, 6, 7 are sealed and not in repo): the phrase 'unprofessional personal communications directed to faculty' appears zero times in Ex. 4, zero times in Ex. 2 (the 18-page complaint compilation most plausibly intended), and zero times in any other exhibit.

- Tab G C15

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

#### F-01 — fabrication

- **Severity:** 4 — severe
- **Filing:** Defendants' Motion to Dismiss (Doc. 27)
- **Signed by:** Scott D. Smith, Assistant Attorney General
- **Location:** p. 16 footnote 5
- **Rule implicated:** Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(3); Tex. Disciplinary R. 3.03(a)(1)
- **Red-team status:** cleared

**Source-text excerpt (what counsel wrote):**

> communications sent directly to faculty members involving bodily fluids, and (iii) vague criticism of COVID-19

**What is wrong with it:**

The words 'crude,' 'bodily,' 'bodily fluids,' 'diarrhea,' and 'vomit' appear zero times in any version of the Complaint. The characterization derives entirely from Defendants' own Exhibits 2 and 8, not from any pleading by Plaintiff. The Rule 11(b)(3) 'factual contention' being the misattribution of exhibit content to the pleading itself.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- R2MTD (Doc. 33) at 10
- Tab G B1
- Rule 11 safe-harbor letter item 1

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

- *Strongest defense:* Defense framing: The Doc. 27 MTD brief is summarizing/characterizing the underlying exhibit content (Exs. 2 + 8 hearing notices), not quoting the Complaint. A reasonable reader of an MTD brief expects counsel to characterize exhibit content when restating the allegations, and Rule 11(b)(3) does not attach to good-faith summarization of attached exhibits even when the summary uses sharper language than the pleading.
- *Why it fails:* The grammatical subject of the operative Doc. 27 sentence (L95-103) is 'Plaintiff' / 'the Complaint', not the exhibits. Counsel is attributing the 'bodily fluids / vomit / diarrhea' characterization TO the pleading. Rule 11(b)(3) attaches to the brief's specific factual contention as written; misattribution of source — claiming the Complaint says X when X appears only in cited exhibits — is the canonical (b)(3) violation. Verified via FAC pp. 6-11 walk: zero occurrences of any of the four characterization words across ¶¶25-37. Three independent rebuttal anchors (R2MTD Doc. 33 at 10, Tab G B1, R11 safe-harbor letter item 1) carry the rebuttal.
- *Catalog confidence:* 0.9

#### F-74 — phantom_citation

- **Severity:** 4 — severe
- **Filing:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50)
- **Signed by:** Scott D. Smith, Assistant Attorney General
- **Location:** p. 13
- **Rule implicated:** Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(3); Tex. Disciplinary R. 3.03(a)(1)
- **Red-team status:** cleared

**Source-text excerpt (what counsel wrote):**

> counsel and full-time government employees for administrative purposes. See, e.g., 1 Tex. Admin. Code § 57.1(12). They do not address litigation authority, conflicts of interest, or the propriety of

**What is wrong with it:**

Verified against the regulation text on Cornell Legal Information Institute: 1 Tex. Admin. Code section 57.1 contains only subsections (1) through (10). There is no subsection (12). Defs cite a non-existent subsection. The actual operative definition is in subsection (6), exactly as Plaintiff's Motion cited: 'Outside Counsel - An attorney or law firm selected by an Agency to provide legal services. The term does not include a full-time employee of the Agency or the Office of the Attorney General.' Defs' (12) cite is to a phantom subsection, while the (6) definition Plaintiff invoked is the controlling text. The phantom-subsection cite functions to evade engagement with the (6) text that on its face defeats Defs' 'Gibson is enough like an employee for the AG to defend him' position.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- 1 Tex. Admin. Code section 57.1(6)
- Cornell LII reproduction of 1 Tex. Admin. Code section 57.1 (subsections 1-10)

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

- *Strongest defense:* Defense framing: Doc. 50's citation to '1 Tex. Admin. Code § 57.1(12)' is a clerical typo for § 57.1(6) — the subsection both parties agree is the 'Outside Counsel' definition. The intended substantive reading of the regulation is unchanged; a typo (12 vs. 6 in a regulation with 10 subsections) is not a Rule 11(b)(3) factual misstatement.
- *Why it fails:* The typo defense is incoherent with the brief's argumentative move. Doc. 50 cites § 57.1(12) precisely to argue that the regulation addresses purposes DIFFERENT from § 57.1(6)'s litigation-authority definition (the subsection Plaintiff invoked). If counsel intended the typo to read § 57.1(6), the brief's logic collapses — counsel would be citing the same subsection they were arguing AGAINST. The phantom subsection is load-bearing for the brief's misdirection, not a clerical slip. Verified against Cornell LII reproduction: § 57.1 contains subsections (1)-(10) only; (12) does not exist. The non-existence of (12) is what enables the brief to attribute 'administrative purposes' content to a subsection-that-isn't, creating the false separation the brief's argument depends on.
- *Catalog confidence:* 0.9

#### F-30 — post_notice_continued_misrep

- **Severity:** 4 — severe
- **Filing:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38)
- **Signed by:** Scott D. Smith, Assistant Attorney General
- **Location:** Throughout
- **Rule implicated:** Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(3); Fed. R. Civ. P. 11(b)(4); Tex. Disciplinary R. 3.03(a)(1)
- **Red-team status:** cleared

**Source-text excerpt (what counsel wrote):**

> these reasons, and those set forth in Defendants’ Motion, Defendants respectfully request that the Court grant their Motion to Dismiss in its entirety and dismiss Plaintiff’s claims with prejudice.

**What is wrong with it:**

Doc. 38 was filed on 2026-03-02 (15 days) after Plaintiff's R2MTD (Doc. 33, filed 2026-02-15) catalogued the Doc. 27 misstatements on the docket. To the extent Doc. 38 re-asserts the same factual contentions without correction or supplemental evidentiary support, those re-assertions occur with actual notice of Plaintiff's catalogued objections. Actual notice is the operative trigger for the Rule 11(c) sanctions analysis even where a single re-assertion does not itself satisfy each element of (b)(3).

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- By existence of Doc. 38 on the docket post-Doc. 33

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

- *Strongest defense:* Defense framing: Doc. 38 is a Reply brief that may legitimately re-assert contested positions; counsel is not required to abandon factual contentions simply because the opposing party files an objection. Rule 11(b)(4) protects good-faith argument that the opposing R2MTD's catalog is wrong. The 'post-notice continuation' framing risks conflating routine adversarial position-holding with (b)(3)/(b)(4) violation, which would chill legitimate reply briefing.
- *Why it fails:* Rule 11(b)(3)/(b)(4) require evidentiary support and warranted-by-existing-law respectively. Once Doc. 33 catalogued specific phantom citations + misattributions with pin-cite verification, continued reliance on those specific items WITHOUT supplemental evidentiary support shifts from contested-good-faith to actual-notice-and-no-corrective-action. The Pickett mischaracterization (Item 52) is canonical: Doc. 38 repeats the same overread of Pickett that Doc. 33 specifically catalogued with the cluster-6477999 opinion text as counter-evidence. The post-notice trigger is specific (per-item) rather than general; this catalog item only attaches when Doc. 38 reasserts items individually catalogued by Doc. 33.
- *Catalog confidence:* 0.75

#### F-43 — overread

- **Severity:** 3 — serious
- **Filing:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50)
- **Signed by:** Scott D. Smith, Assistant Attorney General
- **Location:** p. 11
- **Rule implicated:** Tex. Disciplinary R. 3.03(a)(1)
- **Red-team status:** cleared

**Source-text excerpt (what counsel wrote):**

> Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377, 389–90 (2012) (qualified immunity analysis focuses on the nature

**What is wrong with it:**

Filarsky holds only that a private contractor may assert qualified immunity as a personal defense; it says nothing about who must furnish counsel. AAG Smith never advanced the Filarsky-specific qualified-immunity argument on Gibson's behalf in 33 pages of MTD briefing; he invokes Filarsky now to defeat disqualification but did not invoke it for Gibson when it would have helped Gibson.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. at 389-90
- Draft Reply ISO Disqualify section V.A

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

- *Strongest defense:* Defense framing: Filarsky v. Delia, 566 U.S. 377, 389-90 (2012), establishes that private contractors who perform government functions can invoke qualified immunity — bearing on whether Defendant Gibson's posture supports unified state representation. Citing Filarsky for the QI-availability proposition is doctrinally uncontroversial.
- *Why it fails:* Filarsky's holding addresses WHO can invoke qualified immunity (a private individual retained by the government may), not WHO must furnish counsel. The leap from 'private contractor may invoke QI' to 'therefore the State may represent that contractor' is not in Filarsky. More acutely: AAG Smith never advanced the Filarsky-specific qualified-immunity argument on Gibson's behalf in 33 pages of MTD briefing — Gibson received no Filarsky-based QI defense. Smith now deploys Filarsky to defeat disqualification while having declined to deploy it for Gibson's actual benefit. Cross-issue inconsistency converts the overread into a sev-3 structural problem about whose interests the citation serves.
- *Catalog confidence:* 0.81

#### F-77 — admission_disguised_as_denial

- **Severity:** 3 — serious
- **Filing:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50)
- **Signed by:** Scott D. Smith, Assistant Attorney General
- **Location:** p. 9
- **Rule implicated:** Tex. Disciplinary R. 3.03(a)(1)
- **Red-team status:** cleared

**Source-text excerpt (what counsel wrote):**

> There are no cross-claims, no finger-

**What is wrong with it:**

The absence of cross-claims and finger-pointing - between an institution and an unindemnified independent contractor whose interests structurally diverge - is the suppressed-defense pattern Plaintiff alleges. Asserted as 'evidence of unity'; functions as evidence of constraint by the conflict.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- Dunton v. County of Suffolk, 729 F.2d 903 (2d Cir. 1984)

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

- *Strongest defense:* Defense framing: The absence of cross-claims and finger-pointing between TTUHSC and Gibson reflects unity of interest. Cross-claims aren't required; their absence is normal in many co-defendant cases. Plaintiff is reading conflict-induced silence into routine pleading economy.
- *Why it fails:* Cross-claims and finger-pointing are routine in co-defendant cases where the parties have divergent structural interests — and the structural divergence between TTUHSC (institutional respondent superior + sovereign immunity, official capacity) and Gibson (unindemnified independent contractor sued in individual capacity for damages under qualified immunity) is exactly the class of divergence Dunton addresses. The absence Defs frame as 'unity' is the suppressed-defense pattern Plaintiff alleges. Same admission-disguised-as-denial class as Item 76 — paired compound signal. Defs' own sentence concedes the conflict's manifestation.
- *Catalog confidence:* 0.8

#### F-58 — misstate_pleading

- **Severity:** 3 — serious
- **Filing:** Defendants' Reply ISO MTD (Doc. 38)
- **Signed by:** Scott D. Smith, Assistant Attorney General
- **Location:** p. 6
- **Rule implicated:** Tex. Disciplinary R. 3.03(a)(1)
- **Red-team status:** cleared

**Source-text excerpt (what counsel wrote):**

> It is clear from Plaintiff's First Amended Complaint that the reasonable interpretation of the Plaintiff's statements caused a disruption.

**What is wrong with it:**

Asserts a contested factual conclusion as a reading of the FAC's face. The FAC pleads the opposite: para 31A ('a short philosophical reflection on mortality that did not name TTUHSC, identify any person, or call for or threaten violence'); para 31B ('TTUHSC's own conduct is inconsistent with any genuine belief that Plaintiff posed an imminent safety risk: throughout the same period, administrators continued to meet with him in ordinary settings; Plaintiff attended the December 11, 2023 hearing without any search of his person or belongings or visible special security measures'); para 31C ('treating it as a Code-of-Conduct threat of harm was unreasonable'). Defs' Doc. 38 framing reverses the FAC's pleading on the reasonableness of the threat characterization.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- E-010 through E-018 (No-Threat Admissions)

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

- *Strongest defense:* Defense framing: 'Reasonable interpretation' is institutional discretion language tied to disciplinary-process deference; Defs argue the institution's threat-characterization was reasonable. That's a merits argument fairly within Defs' brief. At Rule 12, the institution's view of reasonableness can be argued; the FAC's view of unreasonableness is for trial.
- *Why it fails:* The brief asserts 'It is clear from Plaintiff's First Amended Complaint' that the disruption inference holds — that is a representation about what the FAC pleads, not about what Defs argue. The FAC pleads the opposite: ¶31A (post 'did not name TTUHSC, identify any person, or call for or threaten violence'); ¶31B (Defs' conduct inconsistent with belief in actual safety risk — continued ordinary meetings, no security at hearing); ¶31C (treating as Code violation was unreasonable). Misframing the FAC's face — not arguing merits — is the candor failure. At Rule 12 the FAC must be taken as pled; the brief reverses it.
- *Catalog confidence:* 0.82

#### F-76 — admission_disguised_as_denial

- **Severity:** 3 — serious
- **Filing:** Defendants' Response in Opposition to Motion to Disqualify (Doc. 50)
- **Signed by:** Scott D. Smith, Assistant Attorney General
- **Location:** p. 11
- **Rule implicated:** Tex. Disciplinary R. 3.03(a)(1)
- **Red-team status:** cleared

**Source-text excerpt (what counsel wrote):**

> TTUHSC has not argued that Gibson acted outside the scope of any engagement, nor has it advanced any defense that would impose liability on Gibson to avoid institutional exposure. Plaintiff's reliance on Dunton therefore rests on a factual predicate that is absent from this case.

**What is wrong with it:**

Defs assert TTUHSC has not argued Gibson acted outside scope as if that absence DISTINGUISHES Dunton. But the absence is the manifestation of the conflict the Motion identifies - TTUHSC, through unified counsel, refuses to make the argument that would help Gibson individually because it would expose the institution. Defs' own sentence is the textbook Dunton admission stated as if exculpatory.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- Dunton v. County of Suffolk, 729 F.2d 903 (2d Cir. 1984)

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

- *Strongest defense:* Defense framing: TTUHSC's choice not to argue Gibson acted outside scope reflects defense strategy. Defs argue this absence DISTINGUISHES Dunton, where the county explicitly invoked scope-out. Strategic choices in litigation aren't admissions; they're tactics. Plaintiff cannot extract a conflict-of-interest from a strategic non-choice.
- *Why it fails:* The Dunton conflict pattern is precisely about counsel being CONSTRAINED from arguments that would help client A because the argument would harm client B. TTUHSC's 'not arguing scope-out' is the constraint, not a distinguishing fact. The absence Defs tout AS exculpatory IS the manifestation of the conflict. Defs' own framing — 'TTUHSC has not argued' — describes the conflict-induced silence. Stated as if exculpatory; functions as textbook admission. Compounding signal: Item 46 catalogues a similar 'strategic choice' framing-as-Dunton-admission. Two independent admission-disguised-as-denial moves in same brief.
- *Catalog confidence:* 0.83

**What is wrong with it:**

Misstates the doctrine. Sovereign immunity is available to TTUHSC and to officials in their official capacity (as an extension of TTUHSC) - but Gibson is sued in his individual capacity only. The 'alignment' Defs assert is impossible because the two co-defendants are litigating fundamentally different defense theories.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- Hafer v. Melo, 502 U.S. 21, 25-26 (1991)

**Red-team test (strongest defense, and why it still fails):**

The brief's 'aligned' framing captures that shared-outcome interest; reading it more narrowly imposes a doctrinal-perfection bar on brief-writing.
- *Why it fails:* Sovereign immunity is NOT an individual-capacity defense (Hafer v. Melo, 502 U.S. at 25-26). Gibson is sued in individual capacity only — sovereign immunity is categorically unavailable to him. The brief explicitly invokes sovereign immunity as 'aligning' the parties' interests; that representation is doctrinally incoherent. TTUHSC litigates sovereign immunity (jurisdictional bar) + failure-to-state; Gibson litigates qualified immunity (merit defense) + failure-to-state. App’x 337, 341 (5th Cir. 2010). Defs deploy Esfeller affirmatively ('the Fifth Circuit held … As a result, Plaintiff cannot establish that the Individual Defendants personally violated clearly established law') in a way that treats it as binding precedent. (b) Shamloo v. Defs cite Shamloo at 521-24 for the narrow proposition that Tinker has been 'applied' to higher-ed, omitting that the 5th Cir. used Tinker's framework to strike down the university's discipline. An honest deployment of Shamloo would acknowledge that the case's outcome cuts against — not for — the proposition that university discipline survives First Amendment scrutiny on QI grounds. (c) Esfeller's factual context is materially distinguishable: an LSU undergraduate engaged in a persistent, on-campus pattern of harassment of a single ex-girlfriend (MySpace and Facebook messages, physical confrontation, threats to her scholarship status, etc.), with an Article-III mootness discussion driven by his post-suit expulsion for low GPA. Bass's complaint pleads a single off-campus social-media post on a matter of public concern by a graduate-professional (medical) student. Defs implicitly cast a private-target harassment case as authority for a public-speech, professional-school discipline case without engaging the doctrinal mismatch.

**Counter-cite / rebuttal anchors:**

- Shamloo v. Miss. State Bd. of Tr. of Insts. of Higher Learning, 620 F.2d 516, 521-24 (5th Cir. 1980) (panel REVERSED district-court denial of preliminary injunction; held Jackson State demonstration regs unconstitutionally vague; plaintiff students prevailed — outcome omitted by Defs)

- *Why it fails:* Three independent overreads stack: (a) Esfeller is unpublished per curiam (391 F. App'x 337); under 5th Cir. Defs deploy Esfeller affirmatively ('the Fifth Circuit held'). Water Code § 49.223(a)'s 'shall be done at the sole expense of the district' language creates a MANDATORY, NON-DISCRETIONARY obligation: 'The use of the word "shall" evidences the mandatory nature of the duty.'
